paragraphs.text: Lesson 43, talking about hypothetical or imaginary situations.
Talking about hypothetical imaginary situations is often one of the most difficult grammar challenges for English learners.
We use the second conditional and third conditional to do this.
Although you may have already studied these structures, hopefully seeing them in conversation and practicing with your own examples will help you remember them better,
so that you can use them more easily in your own speaking.
Conversation number one, imagining that the present was different.
Carrie is a famous actress who is being interviewed on a radio show.
At the end of the show, the interviewer asks her some questions that were sent in by fans.
All the questions are about imaginary situations.
Before we wrap up the show, I have a few interesting questions from our listeners.
Would you mind answering a couple of them?
Not at all. Let's hear them.
Okay, the first one is, if you had to pick a different career, which one would you choose?
If I weren't an actress, I'd be a veterinarian.
That's quite a departure from acting. You wouldn't stay in show business as a director or something like that?
No, I've always loved acting, but I've never liked the entertainment industry in general. It's too competitive and stressful, but I love animals, so yes, I'd be a vet.
Very interesting. The next question comes from a listener in Oakland. She writes,
If you could change one thing about your life, what would it be?
That one's easy. I'd like to have more free time.
So let's say you have the next four weeks off with no commitments whatsoever. What would you do?
Well, I could do a lot of things. Travel, redecorate my house, spend time with my family. It would be hard to choose.
But right now, I'd say I'd probably take a trip to a country where no one knows me, so I could just relax and enjoy.
Our final question is a very creative one. If you had a time machine and you could live in any century you wanted, which one would it be?
I'd live in the future. That time machine goes forward, too, right?
I assume it does.
I wouldn't go back to the past. Although there have been some fascinating periods in history, I wouldn't be able to live without much.
I'm not a modern creature comforts, so I'd travel to the future instead.
That works. Okay, that's all we have time for today. Thanks so much for coming on the show, Carrie.
Conversation phrases.
Let's look at the situations from this dialogue, which Carrie is imagining to be different.
The real situation in the present is, I am an actress.
The imaginary situation is, if I weren't an actress, I'd be a vet.
The real situation in the present is, I have little free time.
The imaginary situation is, if I had more free time, I'd travel.
The real situation in the present is, I don't have a time machine.
The imaginary situation is, if I had a time machine, I'd live in the future.
In all three cases, Carrie is imagining what would happen if something in the present was different.
This difference can be impossible, as in the example of the time machine, or simply unreal or unlikely, as in the example of changing careers or getting more free time.
This type of structure is called the second conditional. You can form the sentences with this formula.
If plus a verb in the simple past, plus the subject, plus would or wouldn't.
Remember that we are imagining that the present was different, even though the verb is in the simple past.
You can also switch the two parts of the sentence or question.
For example, if you won the lottery, what would you do?
Is the same as, what would you do if you won the lottery?
If I won the lottery, I'd buy a boat.
Is the same as, I'd buy a boat if I won the lottery.
Three other ways to phrase the imaginary situation are, let's say, imagine, and what if?
And these are followed by a verb in the simple past.
For example, let's say you had a time machine. What century would you live in?
Imagine you lost all your money. What would you do to survive?
What if your kids were caught stealing? What would you say to them?
To answer a hypothetical question, we use, I'd, and I wouldn't, for saying what you would definitely do, or definitely wouldn't do.
I could, and I might, for saying what is possible to do, but not your definite action.
For example, if I found someone's wallet on the street, I could keep the money, but I wouldn't do that.
I'd give it to the police.
As you can see, could express the possibilities, but would and wouldn't express the definite actions in that imaginary situation.
Conversation number two, imagining that the past was different.
Now the interviewer is talking to Olivia, a successful business woman who founded a multi-million dollar company.
They are talking about how Olivia's life would have been different if certain things had happened in the past.
So tell me, Olivia, what has been one of the big turning points in your life?
Right after graduating from college, I applied for my dream job at a big corporation, and I didn't get it, and that was when I decided to go into business for myself.
If you had gotten that job, you probably wouldn't have started your company.
That's right. My company started very small. It took about ten years to reach a point where it was really profitable.
If I'd had a lot of money to invest in it, then it might have grown faster.
Do you ever regret not taking the more traditional route and just finding another job?
No, not really. I like working for myself. And on a personal note, I actually got to know my husband at an entrepreneurship conference.
If I hadn't gone to the conference, I wouldn't have met him.
I guess not. Could you tell us about one of the problems you've had in your business?
One mistake we made in the early days was buying the absolute cheapest material for our products.
If we'd invested a little more in higher quality material, we could have sold our products at higher prices, and we would have made more profit in the beginning.
Right. Who would you say has been the biggest inspiration to you in your life as an entrepreneur?
I would say my grandmother. She's not an entrepreneur herself, but she's always believed in me. If not for her encouragement, I probably wouldn't have had the courage to pursue my goals.
Conversation phrases. Again, let's take the real situations in the past and compare them with the situations that Olivia is imagining.
The real situation in the past is, I didn't get the job. The imaginary situation is, if I had gotten that job, I probably wouldn't have started the company.
The real situation in the past was, I didn't have money to invest in my company. The imaginary situation is, if I'd had a lot of money to invest in it, then it might have grown faster.
The real situation in the past was, I went to a conference and met my husband. The imaginary situation is, if I hadn't gone to the conference, I wouldn't have met my husband.

The real situation in the past was, we didn't invest in high quality material. And the imaginary situation is, if we'd invested in higher quality material, we could have invested in high quality material.
We could have sold our products at higher prices, and we would have made more profit in the beginning.
The real situation in the past was, my grandmother encouraged me. And here's the imaginary situation. If not for her encouragement, I probably wouldn't have had the courage to pursue my goals.
This structure is called the third conditional, and it is used for talking about how other things in the past would have been different, if one thing had been different.
The basic structure is, if plus the past perfect, plus the subject, plus would have, could have, or might have, plus the past participle.

Would is more certain, and could and might are less certain. Would have is more certain, and could have, or might have, are less certain. Again, we can switch the two parts of the sentence with no change in meaning.
If I hadn't gone to the conference, I wouldn't have met my husband. Is the same as, I wouldn't have met my husband if I hadn't gone to the conference.
In the last question about Olivia's grandmother, she uses a shortened form. If not for. You can use this expression followed by a noun.

For example, if we hadn't had the map, we would have gotten lost. Is the same as, if not for the map, we would have gotten lost. If you hadn't helped me, I wouldn't have succeeded. Is the same as, if not for your help, I wouldn't have succeeded.

These structures can be confusing, so it's essential to practice creating your own sentences. Today's homework is to answer the questions in the lesson text, using sentences in the second and third conditional.
You can send me a recording of your answers by clicking the link in the lesson text, or email them to me at homework-at-aspresso-english.net.
